title: Philip and James (3 May)
hook: Philip asks show us the Father, and James leads the church of Jerusalem

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph the Worker, the carpenter at his bench on the first of May. Your line was work is holy. Which dull task did you do slowly and well? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

It's the last night before the cross. Jesus has washed their feet and is talking about leaving. He says they know the way to where he's going. Thomas has already said, honestly, that they don't. Then Philip speaks up. He doesn't ask for a miracle or a seat in the kingdom. He asks for one thing, and adds that it would be enough. Two apostles share a feast on the third of May, and one of them is remembered for asking to see God. Today, Philip and James.
screen: `THE LAST NIGHT.` → `THOMAS: WE DON'T KNOW THE WAY.` → `PHILIP HAS ONE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here is Philip's request in the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it is enough for us." It's a hungry question. Just let us see God, once, and we'll ask for nothing else. And Jesus answers with a question of his own. Have I been with you so long, Philip, and you haven't known me? Then: "Philip, he that seeth me seeth the Father also." Catholics hear in that line one of the deep claims of their faith: that in Jesus, God has a face. On that reading, there is no climbing past him to reach the Father, and Philip had been looking at the answer for years. The other apostle today is James, whom Mark's Gospel calls James the less. The Latin tradition identifies him with James, son of Alphaeus, from the lists of the twelve, and also with the James whom Paul calls the brother of the Lord, the one who speaks with authority at the council in Jerusalem in Acts. Scholars and churches don't all agree that these are one man, and the Gospels don't settle it. What the Church does with the two of them is pair them on one day, and the pairing works. Philip asks to see. James, in the tradition, stays, and serves the church in Jerusalem, in the city where it all happened. One asks the question. The other, tradition says, spends his life in the city where, for Catholics, the answer stood. Some Catholics pray Philip's line as it is, a whole prayer in a sentence.
screen: `PHILIP: SHOW US THE FATHER.` · `WHO SEES ME SEES THE FATHER.` · `WHICH JAMES? TRADITION SAYS ONE MAN.` · `ONE ASKS; ONE STAYS AND SERVES.` · then, large: `LORD, SHEW US THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to be shown. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Philip didn't dress his question up, so don't dress yours up either. If you pray, you can say his line slowly, Lord, show us the Father, and then stop talking and wait. If you don't pray, ask the plainest version of your own biggest question, the one you rarely say aloud, and then sit with it open, without rushing to answer it. Notice what is already in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Philip and James. Two apostles on one feast: Philip, who asked to see the Father, and James, whom tradition remembers leading the church in Jerusalem.
Your line: show us the father. Today, ask one honest question out loud, to God or to a friend, instead of pretending you already know. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saints Philip and James as one feast on 3 May, with readings that often include Philip's request in John 14; the apostles are honored together in the Mass of the day.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of John 14:8–9 exactly; 14:9 is partly paraphrased ('Have I been with you so long...').
James 'the Less' (Mark 15:40): meaning of 'less' (younger/smaller) given as uncertain. Confirm.
Identification of James son of Alphaeus with James 'brother of the Lord' and leader in Jerusalem is the Latin tradition; stated as tradition and as debated. Confirm fair framing.
Greek of John 14:8 and transliteration: confirm.
'Some Catholics pray Philip's line as it is': confirm or cut.
Editor: cut the superlative 'biggest question in the room', the unsourced guess at why James is called 'the less' (claims rule), and the mind-reading 'close to sadness'.

Audit: 'You don't have to climb past him to find the Father' and 'the place where the answer stood' spoke the belief in the narrator's own voice; now framed as the Catholic reading ('on that reading', 'for Catholics'). DR John 14:8–9 and Mark 15:40 checked.
